html:
By the early 1700s Edo, the shogun's capital and the future Tokyo, had over a million people, which probably made it the largest city in the world at the time.

The growth followed from politics. Under the system of alternate attendance, every lord in Tokugawa Japan had to keep a great house in Edo, live there every other year and leave his family there. Tens of thousands of samurai and servants came with them. Merchants, craftsmen and labourers followed to feed, clothe and serve them. About half the people were samurai households; the other half were crowded into the townsmen's quarters. A census of 1721 counted roughly half a million commoners, not counting samurai.

Edo fed itself through rice shipped by sea from Osaka and the north, and had its own popular culture of kabuki, woodblock prints and fast food such as nigiri sushi. Its frequent great fires, such as that of 1657, were a constant danger. Only after 1868 was it renamed Tokyo.
sum: By the early 1700s Edo, the shogun's capital and the future Tokyo, had over a million people, which probably made it the largest city in the world at the time.
